Economy: stocks jump on Democrat sweep; oil slides as Vance blames Iran war; BMW warns/8k cuts; CVS to split. stories.headline: US stocks jump after Democrats’ midterm sweep; Dow nearly +3%, dollar slides
stories.dek: Investors bet a divided Washington will restrain Trump’s policymaking. Oil also fell hard as markets priced a possible wind-down of the Iran war.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday, after Democrats won both the House and the Senate, US stocks bounced. The Dow Jones rose close to 3% — its best day in more than a year — while the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 each gained about 1.5%. Overnight futures had fallen on election-result nerves, then reversed. The idea: if Congress is not fully controlled by Trump’s party, big swings in trade, taxes and foreign policy may be harder to push through. The US dollar slipped to a one-month low against major currencies. Trump posted that the market hit a record and credited himself; traders pointed more to the ‘divided government’ bet.
stories.why_it_matters: When US indexes swing, Taiwan’s market, pension funds and the New Taiwan dollar often move the next morning. A calmer dollar and cheaper oil can ease some global inflation pressure — but only if the politics stay orderly.
stories.camps: Bulls say divided government means moderation. Bears say policy fights (debt ceiling, spending) could still shock markets. Trump allies claim the rally proves his economic brand; critics say markets are cheering limits on him.
stories.image_alt: US stocks and dollar reaction to midterm results

terms.explain: Index of 30 large US companies.
US index packed with tech stocks.
Index of 500 big US firms; a common ‘the market’ gauge.
When the White House and Congress are led by different parties.

stories.headline: Oil slides below $90 as Vance says the Iran war caused the GOP midterm loss
stories.dek: WTI closed at $88.12 (−8.3%); Brent settled at $94.62 (−8.7%). Markets price a faster path to talks if Democrats press Trump.
stories.caveman: Crude prices tumbled Wednesday. US West Texas Intermediate fell 8.3% to $88.12 a barrel; international Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62. Vice President JD Vance posted that ‘the reason we lost is the war,’ echoing Trump. Traders read Democrat control of Congress as leverage to push for an end to the unpopular Iran conflict that had helped spike gasoline and diesel. Cheaper oil can cool inflation — but the war itself is not over, so prices can snap back on any new strike news.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan imports almost all its energy. Big oil moves change electricity fuel costs, airline tickets and the trade balance.
stories.camps: Hawks say cutting oil now rewards Tehran. Doves say voters already rejected the war at the ballot box. Oil traders just watch whether ceasefire talk becomes real policy.

terms.explain: West Texas Intermediate, the main US oil benchmark.
The main international oil price.

stories.headline: BMW issues second profit warning this year; 8,000 job cuts and China sales slump
stories.dek: Margin guide slashed to between −0.5% and 0.5%. China sales down 22% in nine months; Mercedes also cut outlook last week.
stories.caveman: German carmaker BMW warned again on profits, blaming restructuring costs that include about 8,000 job cuts at home and fierce competition from lower-cost Chinese rivals. It cut its full-year profit margin outlook to a band around zero (−0.5% to 0.5%), after once hoping for 4–6%. Third-quarter pre-tax earnings fell 11% to €2.1bn. China sales dropped 22% in the first nine months. Mercedes-Benz cut its outlook last week too. Western brands are losing share in China and facing more Chinese exports into Europe.
stories.why_it_matters: Germany’s auto industry is a pillar of Europe’s economy. Job cuts there ripple through suppliers — including electronics and parts firms tied to Asia.
stories.camps: Management says cuts are needed to survive. Unions warn of hollowed-out factories. Some European politicians want tougher trade defenses against Chinese EVs; free-traders warn of a tariff war.
stories.image_alt: BMW factory and restructuring context

terms.explain: A company telling investors profits will be worse than expected.
Profit as a share of sales. Near 0% means almost no profit.
Reorganizing a company, often with layoffs and plant changes.

stories.headline: CVS plans to split pharmacies from insurance by 2028, unwinding its $78bn Aetna deal
stories.dek: About 9,000 drugstores would separate from the Aetna insurance arm and Caremark PBM. Shares fell on the news.
stories.caveman: CVS Health said it plans to become two public companies by the first half of 2028: one focused on retail pharmacies, the other on insurance (Aetna) and the pharmacy benefit manager Caremark. That would reverse the giant 2018 merger that bought Aetna for about $78 billion. The board called it the result of a strategic review. Breaking up huge health conglomerates is meant to unlock value — or to escape regulatory heat — but splits are messy and take years.
stories.why_it_matters: Pharmacy and insurance giants shape what medicines cost in the US. A breakup could change drug prices, drugstore jobs and how Taiwanese and global drugmakers get paid.
stories.camps: Investors sometimes cheer breakups as ‘focus.’ Workers fear store closures. Critics of PBMs hope a split brings scrutiny; defenders say vertical integration cut costs.
stories.image_alt: CVS drugstore branding

terms.explain: Pharmacy benefit manager — middlemen that negotiate drug prices for insurers.
CVS’s big health-insurance arm.
One company owning several steps of the same industry chain.

stories.headline: Voters reject data-center projects in 40 of 41 local ballot fights across 10 states
stories.dek: Ohio alone had 21 measures. Only Harwood, North Dakota, went the other way. AI building boom meets local power and land backlash.
stories.caveman: On election night, communities voted on 41 local measures in 10 states that would restrict new data centers — the giant computer warehouses that train AI. According to Ballotpedia and CNBC, voters sided against data centers in all but one race (Harwood, North Dakota). Ohio had more than half the measures. Democrat Sherrod Brown even beat a Republican senator after casting him as ‘the face of data centers.’ Locals often cite power bills, water use and noise; tech firms say the centers bring tax revenue and AI jobs.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan builds many of the AI servers that fill these halls. If US towns keep saying no, cloud companies may shift sites — or push harder into places that say yes.
stories.camps: Tech lobbyists call the votes short-sighted. Environmental and ratepayer groups say communities should not subsidize Big Tech’s electricity. Local officials are stuck between tax promises and angry neighbors.
stories.image_alt: Data center facility exterior

terms.explain: Huge building full of servers that run cloud and AI workloads.
A yes/no question put directly to voters, not just candidates.
A household or business that pays the electric bill.

stories.headline: Qualcomm stock drops 7% after soft outlook; memory chip shortage squeezes phone makers
stories.dek: Quarterly results beat estimates, but guidance lagged. Smartphone SoC demand is shaky as pricier memory forces hard choices.
stories.caveman: Chip designer Qualcomm beat Wall Street’s quarterly numbers, then guided softer than hoped for the current quarter (EPS $2.15–$2.35, revenue $10.4–$11.2bn). Shares fell about 7% after hours. Most of Qualcomm’s chips go into smartphones. That market is messy: memory chips used in phones and AI servers have soared in price, so handset brands cut features or delay launches. Apple had already warned about memory costs; Qualcomm’s forecast shows the pain spreading across Android too.
stories.why_it_matters: Phone demand and memory prices hit Taiwan’s DRAM/NAND and assembly chain. When Qualcomm stumbles, it often foreshadows slower handset builds.
stories.camps: Bulls say AI PCs and auto chips can diversify Qualcomm. Bears say phones are still the cash engine and memory inflation is not done. Consumer advocates note pricier phones hurt ordinary buyers first.
stories.image_alt: Qualcomm chip and smartphone context

terms.explain: US company that designs many Android phone chips and modems.
DRAM/NAND chips that store data; AI data centers are buying huge volumes.
What a company predicts for the next quarter.

stories.headline: SpaceX hires Qualcomm to help build US terrestrial network for Starlink Mobile
stories.dek: Multi-year deal aims to complement satellite links and challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile; rollout eyed next year.
stories.caveman: SpaceX said Qualcomm will supply key network technology for Starlink Mobile, Elon Musk’s planned phone service. Qualcomm said the ground network will ‘complement Starlink’s satellite capabilities,’ with rollout targeted to begin next year. Terms were not disclosed. The pitch: phones that keep working by hopping between cell towers and satellites. Incumbent carriers already partner with satellite firms for emergency texting; a full Musk rival would be a bigger fight over spectrum, towers and regulation.
stories.why_it_matters: Satellite-to-phone needs chips, ground gear and launch capacity — supply chains that often run through Taiwan and the US. It also raises questions about space junk and rural coverage promises.
stories.camps: Fans say competition could lower prices in dead zones. Telecom unions and carriers warn of cherry-picking and safety oversight. Regulators will decide how much spectrum Starlink Mobile can use.
stories.image_alt: SpaceX and mobile network imagery

terms.explain: SpaceX’s satellite internet constellation.
Normal ground cell towers and gear, not satellites.
Radio frequencies governments license for mobile service.

stories.headline: Apple and big cloud stocks surge as midterms remove ‘uncertainty’ premium
stories.dek: Amazon +8%, Google +6%, Apple nearly +7%, Microsoft +4% in Wednesday trade after Democrats flip Congress.
stories.caveman: Big US tech names ripped higher Wednesday once midterm results looked clear. Amazon jumped about 8%, Alphabet (Google) over 6%, Apple nearly 7%, Microsoft about 4%, Meta about 3%. Strategists said election uncertainty lifting can help risk assets; some also argue divided government means ‘moderation’ on taxes and AI rules — though Democrats gaining oversight could mean more hearings for tech CEOs. Separately, European cyber news (hacked blood-bank freezers in France) reminded markets that digital risk is not only a stock story.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan’s foundries and server makers live on hyperscaler capex. A US tech rally often lifts TSMC-supply names the next session — until regulation talk returns.
stories.camps: Bulls call it relief. Skeptics say nothing about AI spending math changed overnight. Progressive Democrats promise tougher tech oversight; companies will lobby hard against it.
stories.image_alt: Big Tech campus and stock surge context

terms.explain: Giant cloud companies like Amazon, Microsoft and Google that buy huge volumes of servers.
Extra caution (or discount) investors demand when politics are unclear.
Google’s parent company.

stories.headline: Democrats seize House and Senate in a blue wave that blindsided Trump’s Maga slate
stories.dek: Party flips multiple deep-red Senate seats (including Texas and Kansas) and two dozen-plus House districts as counting continues.
stories.caveman: Americans woke Wednesday to a radically different map. Democrats took both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats — including deep-red Texas and Kansas — and more than two dozen House districts, with some races still counting. Trump’s handpicked Maga candidates were swept aside. Trump’s first public remarks came from the construction site of his White House ballroom, sidestepping the scale of the loss. The result gives Democrats subpoena power, budget leverage and a chance to block or reshape White House priorities for the next two years.
stories.why_it_matters: US congressional control shapes Taiwan arms sales, China tariffs and global aid. A Democratic Congress can investigate and constrain a Trump second-term agenda.
stories.camps: Democrats call it a mandate on costs, democracy and war. Trump allies blame the Iran war, Fox News or turnout quirks. Historians note midterms often punish the president’s party — this swing was still unusually large.
stories.image_alt: Supporters celebrate Democratic midterm gains

terms.explain: Slang for a big night of Democratic wins.
The two chambers of the US Congress.
A legal order to hand over documents or testify.

stories.headline: JD Vance: ‘The real reason we lost is the war’ with Iran
stories.dek: Vice president distances himself from the conflict ahead of a possible 2028 run; Trump had also called Iran ‘a piece of it.’
stories.caveman: Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the war against Iran was the ‘real reason’ Republicans lost the midterms. In a long post on X he urged colleagues to admit the cost — including losing the Senate for years — if they still think the war was worth it. Vance had earlier been linked to deal-making tracks with Tehran; Trump told the Wall Street Journal that Iran was ‘a piece of’ the defeat. The comments open an intraparty fight: stay the course, or pivot before 2028.
stories.why_it_matters: US-Iran fighting shakes oil, shipping through Hormuz and Asia’s security planning. Taiwan watches any US bandwidth shift away from the Indo-Pacific.
stories.camps: War supporters say retreat would embolden Iran. Opponents say voters already delivered a verdict. Vance’s rivals may paint him as disloyal; his allies say he is being honest.
stories.image_alt: JD Vance speaking on the campaign trail

terms.explain: US vice president under Trump.
Next scheduled US presidential election year.
Fight inside the same political party.

stories.headline: House Speaker Mike Johnson will not stay as top House Republican after the rout
stories.dek: NPR: a source familiar with his plans says he will step aside as GOP leader in the new Congress.
stories.caveman: After Republicans’ bruising midterm defeat, House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana does not plan to remain the party’s top House leader in the next Congress, a source familiar with his plans told NPR. Johnson had stuck close to Trump. Losing the speakership path is normal after a wave election — but the scramble to replace him will show whether House Republicans want a Trump loyalist, a deal-maker, or someone who can work with a Democratic majority.
stories.why_it_matters: Who leads the House minority shapes shutdown fights, Ukraine/Taiwan aid votes and investigations. Leadership chaos can freeze US legislating for weeks.
stories.camps: Trump allies may demand a more combative face. Institutionalists want someone who can cut deals. Democrats will exploit GOP infighting either way.
stories.image_alt: House Speaker Mike Johnson with reporters

terms.explain: Leader of the US House; second in line to the presidency after the vice president.
Top leader of the party that does not hold the chamber majority.

stories.headline: Israel’s president starts coalition talks after another election deadlock
stories.dek: Isaac Herzog received official results and began consulting parties on who can form a government.
stories.caveman: Israeli President Isaac Herzog began consultations with political parties after receiving official results from a general election that again produced no clear winner. Israel’s multi-party system often needs weeks of bargaining to build a majority coalition. Deadlock means caretaker governance, delayed budgets and uncertainty over Gaza policy, Lebanon tensions and relations with Washington — especially as the US itself just flipped partisan control.
stories.why_it_matters: Middle East stability affects oil, shipping and US diplomatic bandwidth. Taiwan’s security planning assumes the US is not permanently stuck elsewhere.
stories.camps: Each Israeli bloc blames the other for refusing compromise. Outside powers push for a stable partner; voters look exhausted by repeat elections.
stories.image_alt: President Isaac Herzog receiving election results

terms.explain: Alliance of parties that together hold a majority.
No side can form a stable majority.
Temporary government with limited powers while talks continue.

stories.headline: HOT: US libraries win big on local ballots — EveryLibrary tracks gains on 41 measures
stories.dek: Alongside the blue wave, voters approved many millages, levies and parcel taxes that fund public libraries.
stories.caveman: Election night was not only about Congress. EveryLibrary, a PAC that backs library funding, said America’s ‘third place’ scored wins on 41 ballot measures nationwide. Over 90% of US library money is set by statehouses or city councils, so referenda and local taxes matter more than presidential tweets. Analysts described stronger budgets that keep ‘stacks in the stacks’ after years of book bans and staff cuts in some states. Lit Hub dubbed it a possible ‘Book Wave.’
stories.why_it_matters: Libraries are where kids get homework help and adults get job-search internet. Funding fights are culture fights about who belongs in public space.
stories.camps: Library advocates call the results a rebuke to censorship campaigns. Critics of tax rises say households are already stretched. Publishers quietly cheer any channel that still lends new books.
stories.image_alt: Illustration related to libraries at the polls

terms.explain: Local tax measures that raise money for a specific service like libraries.
Political action committee that raises money for causes or candidates.
A community spot that is not home or work — cafes, libraries, parks.

stories.headline: HOT: Sarah J Maas’s new ACOTAR novel is UK’s fastest-selling adult fantasy since 1998
stories.dek: A Court of Splintered Harmony sold 188,914 UK copies in days; US romantasy star still sets the pace globally.
stories.caveman: US author Sarah J Maas returned to her A Court of Thorns and Roses series after five-plus years. A Court of Splintered Harmony sold 188,914 copies in the UK between 27 and 31 October, NielsenIQ BookData said — the fastest-selling adult fantasy novel since records began in 1998, beating Rebecca Yarros’s Onyx Storm (155,141). It was also the biggest adult-fiction hardback week in the UK since Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman in 2015. Harry Potter still holds broader fantasy weekly records, but for adult fantasy Maas now leads. Romantasy (romance + fantasy) remains publishing’s hottest commercial engine.
stories.why_it_matters: When one US author moves this many hardbacks, printers, translators, film scouts and bookstore chains all rearrange schedules — including in Asia.
stories.camps: Fans celebrate. Some literary critics sniff at romantasy’s formula. Booksellers like the traffic even if they wish taste were broader.

stories.headline: HOT: William T Vollmann’s 3,000-page A Table for Fortune tries to reckon with America at 250
stories.dek: Guardian review: a huge, CIA-voiced, myth-heavy novel about the US experiment — ambitious, exhausting, hard to ignore.
stories.caveman: As the United States marks roughly 250 years since its founding myths, American novelist William T Vollmann publishes A Table for Fortune, a roughly 3,000-page novel that reviewers describe as a sprawling portrait of national rise and decline. Sections adopt institutional voices (including a CIA-like narrator). It is the opposite of a quick beach read: maximalist, research-heavy, argumentative about violence and empire. Whether readers finish it or not, the review attention puts serious US literary ambition back in the window beside commercial romantasy.
stories.why_it_matters: Big literary events set syllabi, translation budgets and prize shortlists. They also remind readers that US fiction is more than BookTok trends.
stories.camps: Admirers call Vollmann necessary and brave. Detractors call the length self-indulgent. Teachers will debate whether assigning even part of it is fair.
stories.image_alt: Artwork related to Vollmann’s novel review

terms.explain: A style that piles on detail, pages and voices instead of cutting to the minimum.
TikTok’s book-recommendation culture, often boosting commercial fiction.

stories.headline: MIXED: Lit Hub Daily roundup — Freud anniversary, book-smell history, translators as ‘archeologists’
stories.dek: A deskful of US literary-internet reading: craft essays, queer fairytales, and a note that translators are not parrots.
stories.caveman: Lit Hub’s November 4 daily mix leans essayistic rather than sales-chart: the anniversary of Freud’s Interpretation of Dreams; a history of how collected books smell; Megan Mayhew on ‘analog minds’ and John Elder’s reading life; Ry Herman on queer fairytales; Olivia Manning’s lightly fictionalized friends; and Ilan Stavans telling emerging translators they are ‘archeologists of our verbal reservoir,’ not parrots. It is a snapshot of the US literary web’s midweek brain — curious, craft-heavy, less algorithmically loud than romantasy charts.
stories.why_it_matters: Daily literary newsletters shape what independent bookstores hand-sell and what MFA students argue about.
stories.camps: Fans of serious craft feel fed. Readers hunting only plot may bounce. The quiet point: translation and criticism still need oxygen beside bestsellers.
stories.image_alt: Lit Hub Daily artwork

terms.explain: Literary Hub, a major US literary news and essay site.
Master of Fine Arts — common creative-writing graduate degree.

stories.headline: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to the UK
stories.dek: UK government confirms a citizen tested positive; patient to receive specialized treatment under strict infection controls.
stories.caveman: A British healthcare worker in the Democratic Republic of the Congo tested positive for Ebola and is being evacuated to the UK for treatment, the government said. Ebola spreads through contact with bodily fluids and can kill, but countries with specialized isolation units can treat patients with lower risk to the public if protocols hold. Officials typically stress that casual contact in the destination country is not how outbreaks start — hospital infection control is the hard part.
stories.why_it_matters: Health-worker infections show the human cost of responding to African outbreaks. Global aviation rules and vaccine stockpiles matter to every hub city, including in Asia.
stories.camps: Public-health agencies urge calm and facts. Panic-prone social media may amplify fear. Aid groups ask donors not to abandon Congo clinics when a case hits the headlines.
stories.image_alt: Medical evacuation / Ebola response context

terms.explain: A severe viral disease that spreads via bodily fluids, not casual air contact.
Democratic Republic of the Congo, a large Central African country.
Moving a patient to another country for care.

stories.headline: US ballot measures: three states protect abortion access; voters also weigh LGBTQ, guns, AI
stories.dek: NPR: 146 statewide measures across 39 states. Missouri rejects a Republican-backed abortion curb; Idaho keeps its ban.
stories.caveman: Beyond candidate races, Americans voted on 146 statewide ballot measures. On abortion, four states voted; three moved to preserve access while Idaho kept its 2022-style ban. Missouri voters rejected a Republican-backed restriction. Other measures touched LGBTQ rights, guns, taxes, traffic cameras and even data centers. Since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, ballots have become a main way states rewrite reproductive rules — and this midterm continued that pattern in a mostly protective direction.
stories.why_it_matters: State ballots now decide rights that federal courts stepped back from. That affects families, travel for care, and how companies set HR policies across US sites.
stories.camps: Abortion-rights groups call it a winning streak. Abortion foes say they will try again with narrower wording. LGBTQ and gun measures show the culture war is fought city by city, not only in Washington.
stories.image_alt: Voters and statewide ballot measures

stories.headline: UNHCR criticises UK plan making refugees wait up to 30 years to settle
stories.dek: Home Office ‘earned settlement’ strategy raises ‘significant concerns,’ the UN refugee agency says.
stories.caveman: The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) criticised a UK government plan that could make refugees wait as long as 30 years before gaining settlement rights. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood unveiled an ‘earned settlement’ approach as part of a wider immigration package that also softens some earlier hard edges. UNHCR says ultra-long waits leave people in limbo — hard to work, study or feel safe — and may clash with refugee-protection norms. Britain remains a rich destination country debating how many people to accept and how fast they become permanent residents.
stories.why_it_matters: Refugee rules in Europe shift migration routes and asylum claims worldwide. Taiwan’s own debates on humanitarian admission watch these precedents.
stories.camps: Restrictionists say long waits deter irregular arrivals. Refugee advocates call 30 years cruel and unworkable. Courts may eventually test the policy.
stories.image_alt: People being processed in UK border setting

terms.explain: UN Refugee Agency.
Permission to stay long-term / permanently.
Protection given to people fleeing danger in their home country.

stories.headline: El Niño ‘burns’ the Pacific: typhoons batter East Asia, killing dozens and shutting airports
stories.dek: BBC: storms hit the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan; Typhoon Champi’s 295 km/h winds briefly threatened all of Taiwan.
stories.caveman: A harsh stretch of storms, worsened by the El Niño climate pattern, has killed dozens and smashed crops, airports and power lines across East Asia. In October, Typhoon Champi — winds near 295 km/h, comparable to a Category 5 hurricane — forced nearly all of Taiwan to shut down as the storm aimed at the north-east coast. Similar extremes hit the Philippines, coastal China and Japan. Scientists warn warmer oceans feed stronger storms; governments argue about seawalls, evacuation drills and cutting emissions at the same time.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan lives on the typhoon path. Each ‘record’ storm is an insurance, agriculture and semiconductor-uptime problem — not just a weather story.
stories.camps: Climate scientists link warmer seas to more intense storms. Some politicians still call any single storm ‘natural variability.’ Coastal communities want concrete protection now, not only 2050 targets.
stories.image_alt: Fishermen under a crimson sky after a super typhoon

terms.explain: A recurring Pacific climate pattern that shifts rainfall and storm behavior worldwide.
The name for hurricanes in the northwest Pacific.
